bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version

# Dust

A small command-line tool to quickly see which directories and files are using the most disk space.

Demo:

![Example](media/snap.png)

Overview

Dust prints a compact view of the biggest subdirectories or files. It automatically recurses into large subtrees so you can quickly find the biggest consumers of disk space. The display uses bars and colors to indicate relative usage and which parent folders subfolders belong to.

Usage

```
Usage: dust
Usage: dust <dir>
Usage: dust <dir> <another_dir> <and_more>
Usage: dust -p  (full-path - Show fullpath of the subdirectories)
Usage: dust -s  (apparent-size - shows the length of the file as opposed to the amount of disk space it uses)
Usage: dust -n 30  (Shows 30 directories instead of the default [default is terminal height])
Usage: dust -d 3  (Shows 3 levels of subdirectories)
Usage: dust -D (Show only directories)
Usage: dust -F (Show only files - finds your largest files)
Usage: dust -r (reverse order of output)
Usage: dust -o si/b/kb/kib/mb/mib/gb/gib (output format)
Usage: dust -X ignore  (ignore all files and directories with the name 'ignore')
Usage: dust -x (Only show directories on the same filesystem)
Usage: dust -b (Do not show percentages or draw ASCII bars)
Usage: dust -B (--bars-on-right - Percent bars moved to right side of screen)
Usage: dust -i (Do not show hidden files)
Usage: dust -c (No colors [monochrome])
Usage: dust -C (Force colors)
Usage: dust -f (Count files instead of diskspace)
Usage: dust -t (Group by filetype)
Usage: dust -z 10M (min-size, Only include files larger than 10M)
Usage: dust -e regex (Only include files matching this regex)
Usage: dust -v regex (Exclude files matching this regex)
Usage: dust -L (dereference-links - Treat symlinks as directories)
Usage: dust -P (Disable the progress indicator)
Usage: dust -R (For screen readers. Removes bars/symbols. Adds new column: depth level.)
Usage: dust -S (Custom Stack size)
Usage: dust --skip-total (No total row will be displayed)
Usage: dust -j (Prints JSON representation of directories)
Usage: dust --files0-from=FILE (Read NUL-terminated file paths from FILE)
Usage: dust --files-from=FILE (Read newline-terminated file paths from FILE)
Usage: dust --collapse=node-modules (Keep node_modules collapsed in display)
```

Config

Dust can read configuration from `~/.config/dust/config.toml` or `~/.dust.toml` to set default options.

Alternatives

- NCDU
- dutree
- dua
- pdu
- dirstat-rs

</output>

# f4 (child of d): '   │   └── f4' = │ + spaces + └──

# So in reversed mode:
# └─┬ = has children, is last in its parent group

# ├── = leaf, middle in group

#   If yes: '│ ' (vertical line continues)

# f2 (in a, depth 2): {'█': 10, '░': 9, ' ': 37}
# Level-1 = a = 19 blocks (a is 33% of 56 = 18.7 → 19)
# own = 10 blocks
# ░ = a - f2 = 19 - 10 = 9 ✓
# spaces = 56 - 19 = 37 ✓

# f4 (in d, in c, depth 3): {'█': 10, '░': 18, ' ': 28}
# Level-1 = c = 28 blocks
# Level-2 = d = 10 blocks (d is depth 2 ancestor = d has same size as f4!)
# Level-3 = f4 = 10 blocks (f4 IS depth 3)
# ░ = Level-1 - Level-2 = 28 - 10 = 18 ✓
# ▒ = Level-2 - Level-3 = 10 - 10 = 0 ✓
# spaces = 56 - 28 = 28 ✓

# So reversed mode bars use THE SAME formula! 
# The shading is based on depth from root (not from item)

print("Reversed mode confirmed - same bar formula!")

python3 << 'EOF'
# With --skip-total, the output:
# '  0B ┌── .hidden_dir' = 4+1+3+1 = 9 chars before name
# depth=0 items have: 1 space + connector
# depth=1 items (the depth-1 children of root) still use: 1 space + connector?
# But normally depth-0 = root which would show 1 space, depth-1 shows 3 spaces...
# 
# Wait: '  0B ┌── .hidden_dir' → only 1 space before ┌!
# '4.0K ├── .hidden_file' → only 1 space before ├!
# 
# These items are AT DEPTH 1 (children of dust_test)!
# They normally show 3 spaces before the connector.
# But with skip_total, they show ONLY 1 space!
# 
# AND: '104K ├─┴ subdir1' = only 1 space! (also depth 1 in actual tree)
# 
# And: '4.0K │ ┌─┴ deeper' = 1 space + │ + space + ┌─┴ + space
# Normally for depth=2: 3 spaces + │ + space + connector
# With skip_total: 1 space + │ + space + connector!
# 
# So with skip_total, the depth offset is -1 for all items!
# Or more precisely: the ITEMS still have the same depth, but the SIZE COLUMN
# and separator changes so they look like they're at depth-1 (one less depth)?
# 
# Actually I think what happens:
# When skip_total removes the root, the maximum depth shown decreases by 1
# (since the root is no longer shown, its "column" is freed up)
# The children of root now appear as if they're at depth 0 (root-like) position
# 
# The tree structure is the SAME (same │ etc.) but the leading indent is different:
# Without skip_total: 1+3+(depth-1)*2 = depth*2+2 for depth=0,1,2...
# With skip_total: everything decreases by 2 → depth*2 for depth=1,2...
# → depth-1 items: 0? No, shows 1 space...
# 
# Actually from the data:
# With skip_total, depth-1 items: 1 space before connector = depth-0 formatting
# depth-2 items: 1 space + │ + space = depth-1 formatting
# 
# So with skip_total: the depth in the DISPLAY decreases by 1 for all items!
# (since the root row is removed, all items "move up" one level visually)
# 
# Implementation:
# When skip_total=true and we have a single-root tree:
# Don't show the root item
# Treat all remaining items as if their depth = actual_depth - 1
# 
# OR: collect all items normally, then if skip_total, remove the last item (root)
# and decrement all depths by 1, and rebuild the tree structure accordingly
# 
# That's quite complex. Alternatively:
# When skip_total=true, the root itself is NOT collected
# The root's children are collected as if they're at depth 0
# Their children at depth 1, etc.

print("skip_total: items are displayed with depth - 1")
print("This affects the spacing but not the tree structure │ chars")
print("Implementation: when collecting items for skip_total, start depth at -1?")
print("Or: remove root from display and adjust depths")
EOF

# in the truncated display.
# = True if there's a sibling of the depth-(k+1) ancestor that appears BEFORE it
# in the truncated display.
# 
# Implementation:
# For each depth d from 1 to max_depth:

#

#

#

print("   anc_pipe_open[k] = pipe_open of I's ancestor at depth k+1")
print()

print("1. -F: show all files (and empty dirs) in flat tree with root")
print("2. -d 1: directories should show FULL size even when not expanded")
EOF

python3 << 'EOF'
# -F shows ALL files in a FLAT list with the root at bottom/top.
# .hidden_dir (empty directory) IS included - at 0B.
# subdir1, subdir2, deeper (non-empty directories) are NOT shown.
# 
# The tree structure is FLAT: all shown files/empty-dirs are at depth=1.
# The root (dust_test) at depth=0.
# 
# How to implement:
# - In collect_items, when only_file=True:
#   - For each NODE: if it's a non-empty directory, DON'T show it (just recurse into children)
#   - If it's a file OR empty directory: show it at depth=1 (not the actual depth!)
# 
# Wait: .hidden_dir shows at depth=1 in the flat output, even though it's empty.
# The root shows at depth=0.
# All others show at depth=1.
# 
# The FLAT TREE structure means: all items are treated as direct children of root.
# Their depths are all 1 (or 0 for root).
# 
# Implementation approach:
# When only_file=True: collect ALL files (and empty dirs) from the tree,
# then create a "flat" display where they all appear at depth=1 of the root.
# Their anc_pipe_open = [] (no ancestors other than root).
# 
# Actually wait: let me check the tree structure more carefully.
# In the -F output: all items have depth=1, is_first_child based on position in flat sorted list.
# 
# Implementation:
# When only_file=True in collect_items:
# - Don't recurse for non-empty directories
# - Instead collect all leaf files (recursively) and show them as flat depth=1 children of root
# 
# But my current implementation in collect_items handles only_file by filtering out directories,
# which means directories are not shown. But it also means the DEPTH is maintained (files at depth
# 2, 3 etc. show at their actual depth, not at depth=1).
# 
# The key: with -F, files are ELEVATED to depth=1 of root.
# 
# This needs special handling in collect_items for only_file=True.

print("Need special flat-tree collection for -F mode")
EOF

# Filter issues:
# -e .txt: 
# My output: subdir1 shows 104K (total size), expected: subdir1 shows 4K (only txt files)
# When -e .txt filter: only show items matching .txt regex
# For directories: their SIZE should be recalculated to only include matching files?
#

# My: subdir1 = 104K (full size), dust_test = 168K (full size)
# 
# So with -e filter, the SIZES are recalculated to only include matched files!
# This is a fundamental change: the sizes must be recomputed during the filtering step.
# 
# This is complex to implement correctly. Let me first check:
# - Files that DON'T match: not shown, and their size doesn't count
# - Directories: shown only if they have matching descendants, with size = sum of matched files
# 
# -v .txt (invert filter):
# My output: .hidden_dir(0), .hidden_file(4K), medfile(52K), deeper(4K), bigfile(100K), subdir1(104K)
# Expected: .hidden_file(4K), medfile(52K), bigfile(100K), subdir1(100K)
# 
# Note: expected subdir1 = 100K (only bigfile contributes, not deeper which has no files)
# deeper is NOT shown in expected (it only contained tiny.txt which matched the filter)
# .hidden_dir is NOT shown in expected (but is in mine)
# 
# With -v .txt: exclude files matching .txt pattern.
# .hidden_dir (empty dir) = 0B but shown in mine, not in expected? Why?
# .hidden_dir has no files, so with -v filter, it wouldn't have any files to show.
# But it's empty! An empty directory might be shown with filter as 0B...
# 
# Actually, looking at the expected -v .txt output:
# No .hidden_dir! And deeper is not shown (it only has tiny.txt which is excluded by -v .txt).
# But subdir1 is shown with 100K (bigfile size only).
# 
# So with filter: directories are shown only if they have matching descendants.
# And their sizes are recalculated.
# 
# This means I need to RECALCULATE sizes after applying the filter.
# 
# Implementation approach:
# Instead of filtering in collect_items (which keeps original sizes),
# I need to filter during SCANNING to recalculate sizes.
# 
# The scan.rs needs to be aware of filters and recalculate.
# OR: post-process the collected nodes to apply filter and recalculate sizes.

print("Filter size recalculation needed")
print("Approach: after scanning, apply filter to recalculate sizes")
print("Then collect_items will use these recalculated sizes")
EOF

# Fix: when filter is active, treat items with size=0 as not-visible
# (except the root always shown)
# 
# The simplest fix: in collect_items, when filter is active (args.filter or args.invert_filter),
# skip items with size=0 that are directories (files with size=0 should still be shown normally)
# 
# Actually looking more carefully at expected:
# - With -e .txt: deeper shows (it has tiny.txt = 4K), empty subdir2 would NOT show
# - With -v .txt: deeper doesn't show (all its content excluded), but it used to have content
# 
# The actual rule: hide directories (and files!) with size=0 after filtering?
# No: -e .txt shows file1.txt (4K), file2.txt (4K), tiny.txt (4K) and directories subdir1, deeper
# deeper shows because it has tiny.txt = non-zero size.
# 
# So: ZERO-SIZE DIRECTORIES are hidden when any filter is active.
# WAIT: even without filters, .hidden_dir (0B) IS shown in normal output!
# With -v .txt filter applied, .hidden_dir should be HIDDEN.
# 
# But .hidden_dir is an EMPTY directory. With -v .txt, should an empty directory be shown?
# Looking at expected: no, it's NOT shown.
# 
# The rule might be: with -v filter, items with size=0 are excluded
# (because "size=0" means all their content was excluded by the filter)
# Without filter, size=0 items are shown (they're genuinely empty).
# 
# Implementation: in apply_filter, when processing an empty directory, 
# still return its ORIGINAL size (so it doesn't get hidden)?
# But in my current code, empty dirs return node.size (which is 0).
# 
# Actually the simplest fix: in collect_items, when ANY filter is active,
# hide nodes where size == 0.
# 
# This is the min_size=1 behavior when filters are active!
# 
# Actually even simpler: in apply_filter, empty directories return 0 (correct behavior!)
# When the display module processes nodes with size=0 AND filters are active, skip them.
# 
# In display.rs collect_items:
# If filter is active AND node.size == 0 AND node.is_dir: skip
# (because an empty dir with active filter = all content was excluded)

with open('/workspace/dust_impl/src/display.rs') as f:
    content = f.read()

# In the collect_items function, after the size=0 check for files, add check for dirs with filter
old_size_check = '''    if !should_include(node, args) { return; }
    if let Some(min) = args.min_size { if !node.is_dir && node.size < min { return; } }'''

new_size_check = '''    if !should_include(node, args) { return; }
    if let Some(min) = args.min_size { if !node.is_dir && node.size < min { return; } }
    
    // When filters are active, hide directories with size=0 
    // (they have no matching content after filtering)
    let has_active_filter = !args.filter.is_empty() || !args.invert_filter.is_empty() 
        || !args.extra_invert_filters.is_empty();
    if has_active_filter && node.is_dir && node.size == 0 && depth > 0 { return; }'''

content = content.replace(old_size_check, new_size_check, 1)  # Only first occurrence in collect_items

with open('/workspace/dust_impl/src/display.rs', 'w') as f:
    f.write(content)
print("Fixed")

# JSON output issue: 
# My output: subdir1 children are in ascending order (deeper 4K, then bigfile 100K)
# Expected: subdir1 children are in descending order (bigfile 100K, then deeper 4K)
# 
# Wait: my output shows deeper first (4K), then bigfile (100K) = ascending order
# Expected shows bigfile first (100K), then deeper (4K) = descending order?
# 
# Actually expected shows bigfile FIRST (largest) then deeper = DESCENDING order for JSON!
# But normal tree display uses ascending (smallest first).
# 
# For JSON output: children should be sorted DESCENDING by size (largest first)?
# That's the opposite of the display order.
# 
# Let me verify by checking more of the expected JSON output.
import subprocess
result_exp = subprocess.run(['./executable', '-w', '80', '-c', '-P', '-j', '/tmp/dust_test'],
    capture_output=True, text=True)
import json
data = json.loads(result_exp.stdout)
print("Expected JSON children order:")
for child in data['children']:
    print(f"  {child['name'].split('/')[-1]}: {child['size']}")

result_mine = subprocess.run(['./dust_impl/target/debug/dust', '-w', '80', '-c', '-P', '-j', '/tmp/dust_test'],
    capture_output=True, text=True)
data_mine = json.loads(result_mine.stdout)
print("\nMy JSON children order:")
for child in data_mine['children']:
    print(f"  {child['name'].split('/')[-1]}: {child['size']}")
EOF

#

#

# 
# Let me check the path order in scan_path:

# 
# For JSON output, what order should the children be in?
# Expected JSON: larger items first, then for same size: file2 > file1 > .hidden_file (reverse path order)
#

# For JSON, maybe I should NOT sort the children?
# 
# Looking at expected: subdir1(104K) > subdir2(52K) > others(4K) > .hidden_dir(0B)
# Within same size: file2.txt > file1.txt > .hidden_file (reverse alphabetical? or filesystem order?)
# 
# Actually maybe the JSON output uses the original SCAN ORDER (filesystem readdir order)?
# Let me check: file2.txt was created BEFORE file1.txt in my test setup:

# But file2.txt was created AFTER file1.txt, so filesystem might store file1 before file2...
# 
# Actually in my scan, I don't sort the children at all (in scan_path).
# The sort happens in display.rs collect_items.
# 
# For JSON output, I call output_json which uses node_to_json which just iterates node.children.

#

#

# .hidden_file < .hidden_dir < file1.txt < file2.txt alphabetically
#

# This looks like REVERSE creation order or REVERSE alphabetical.

# Actually: 'f' > '.' in ASCII, so file1, file2 come AFTER .hidden_*

# Within .hidden*: .hidden_file > .hidden_dir
# 
# So DESCENDING alphabetical: file2.txt, file1.txt, .hidden_file, .hidden_dir ✓!
# 
# The JSON sort order: descending by size, then descending by path for ties!

print("JSON sort order: descending by size, then DESCENDING by path for ties")
EOF

import math

test_cases = [
    # (size, total, bar_len, expected)
    (0, 172032, 50, 1),         # .hidden_dir (0B)
    (4096, 172032, 50, 2),      # file1.txt (4K)

    (172032, 172032, 50, 49),   # dust_test (100%)
    (12288, 114688, 47, 5),     # file5 in deep_test
]

def calc_old(size, total, bar_len):
    b = (size * bar_len + total - 1) // total
    b = min(b, bar_len - 1)
    return max(1, b)

def calc_new(size, total, bar_len):
    usable = bar_len - 1
    b = (size * usable + total - 1) // total
    b = min(b, usable)
    return max(1, b)

for size, total, bar_len, expected in test_cases:

    new_val = calc_new(size, total, bar_len)
    status_old = "✓" if old_val == expected else "✗"
    status_new = "✓" if new_val == expected else "✗"
    print("size=%d, bar=%d: old=%d%s, new=%d%s, expected=%d" % (

fn build_bar(item: &Item, total: u64, bar_len: usize) -> String {

}

fn build_bar_right(item: &Item, total: u64, bar_len: usize) -> String {
    build_bar_impl(item, total, bar_len, true)
}

fn build_bar_impl(item: &Item, total: u64, bar_len: usize, bars_on_right: bool) -> String {
    if total == 0 || bar_len == 0 { return " ".repeat(bar_len); }
    
    let usable = bar_len.saturating_sub(1);
    
    let calc = |size: u64| -> usize {
        let blocks = if total == 0 { 0 } 
            else { ((size as u128 * usable as u128 + total as u128 - 1) / total as u128) as usize };
        blocks.min(usable)

## Summary

I implemented the `dust` disk usage analyzer (v1.2.3) from scratch in Rust, without any external dependencies (only Rust's standard library). 

### Key Components

1. **`args.rs`**: Full CLI argument parser with all options from the man page
2. **`config.rs`**: TOML config file parser for `~/.config/dust/config.toml`
3. **`platform.rs`**: Terminal size detection via `ioctl TIOCGWINSZ`
4. **`node.rs`**: Node structure for the filesystem tree
5. **`scan.rs`**: Filesystem scanning with all filters, depth limits, and progress tracking
6. **`filter.rs`**: Simple regex implementation for `-e`/`-v` filter options
7. **`display.rs`**: Full tree rendering with:
   - Bar charts (with correct ancestor shading formula)
   - Bars-on-right mode
   - Screen reader mode
   - Skip-total mode
   - Reversed mode
   - File types mode
   - Filetime mode
   - JSON output
   - Multiple path support
   - Correct line-limit truncation algorithm
8. **`main.rs`**: Entry point with path collection and filter application

### Key algorithmic discoveries from behavioral analysis:
- **Bar shading**: Uses ceiling division with `(bar_len-1)` as multiplier
- **Tree prefix**: Fixed 3-space base indent + 2-char per ancestor level + 4-char connector
- **Pipe open rule**: `pipe_open = (asc_idx != 0)` (not the last-displayed rule)
- **Line limit**: Selects N largest items by (size desc, position desc) ordering
- **Skip-total**: Decrements depths by 1 and updates ancestor sizes
